direct_answer: A static bike or pedal exerciser can be a low-impact way to keep knees and hips moving with osteoarthritis. Start gently, set the seat at the right height and make getting on and off safe. Ask a physiotherapist if you are unsure.

content:
Cycling is low impact and can be done indoors.

This guide covers safe use. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Getting on and off safely

  • Recumbent bikes are easier to mount.
  • A pedal exerciser can be used from a chair.

Set-up

Seat height should allow a slight bend in the knee.

Starting

  • A few minutes at low resistance.
  • Build up slowly.

When to stop

  • Chest pain, dizziness or breathlessness: stop and seek help.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is cycling good for knee OA?

Exercise is a core treatment for OA.

How often?

Little and often.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Osteoarthritis
  • NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s
  • NHS: Physical activity guidelines for older adults

If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111 (NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland; in Northern Ireland, your GP or GP out-of-hours service).
